balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revpar.title: RevPAR, ADR and Occupancy
revpar.content:
RevPAR (revenue per available room) is ADR (average daily rate) × Occupancy -- the single best proxy for hotel-level demand, independent of how many rooms Hilton adds.

For Hilton: Hilton earns franchise and management fees as a percentage of hotel-level revenue, so system-wide RevPAR, not Hilton's own revenue line, is the real driver of fee income. Management guided FY2026 system-wide comparable RevPAR growth of 4.0%-4.5% (raised from 3.0%-3.5%), with Q4 2026 alone guided at only 3.0%-3.5% on US midterm-election and Middle East headwinds.

What to watch:

  • Occupancy vs ADR -- rate-led RevPAR growth is higher-margin than occupancy-led growth
  • US RevPAR (ADRUS/RevPARUS columns) vs system-wide, since the US is Hilton's largest and most mature market
  • Quarterly deceleration flagged against full-year guidance

pipeline.title: Net unit growth and development pipeline
pipeline.content:
Net unit growth (NUG) is the annual percentage increase in system rooms after openings and removals. The pipeline is hotels signed but not yet open -- the leading indicator for NUG one to three years out.

For Hilton: this is the core of the asset-light growth algorithm -- Hilton funds almost none of the construction, it just signs the brand and collects fees once a hotel opens. TTM NUG was 6.0% as of Q3 2026 against a record pipeline of ~3,869 hotels / ~543,100 rooms, nearly half under construction and more than half outside the US; management guides 6%-7% NUG for several years on the strength of that pipeline.

What to watch:

  • Pipeline growth stalling while NUG holds up -- a sign today's growth is outrunning tomorrow's
  • Conversion brands (Curio, Tapestry, Spark, DoubleTree) adding rooms with no new construction
  • International share of the pipeline vs the more mature, slower-growing US

systemSize.title: System size: hotels and rooms
systemSize.content:
System hotels and system rooms are the installed base Hilton earns franchise and management fees on -- the denominator that NUG and the pipeline grow.

For Hilton: most new fee revenue comes from adding rooms to this base, not from raising fees on existing ones, so the slope of this line is closer to a long-run fee-revenue growth rate than RevPAR is on its own.

What to watch:

  • Rooms growing faster than hotels (larger average property size, e.g. new-build full-service vs conversions)
  • New formats (LivSmart Studios, Apartment Collection launched January 2026) adding brands without yet moving the room count materially

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: management & franchise vs ownership
segmentRevenue.content:
Hilton reports management & franchise fee revenue separately from the small ownership segment, where Hilton still owns or leases a handful of hotels directly.

For Hilton: the mix-shift toward management & franchise is the thesis -- fee revenue scales with system rooms and RevPAR at near-zero incremental capital, while ownership revenue is capital-intensive and structurally shrinking as a share of the total.

What to watch:

  • Ownership's shrinking share of total segment revenue over time
  • Management & franchise revenue growing faster than system rooms (fee-rate or ancillary licensing upside, e.g. co-brand card and HGV timeshare fees)

segmentEbitda.title: Segment Adjusted EBITDA: management & franchise vs ownership
segmentEbitda.content:
The same split as segment revenue, but on Adjusted EBITDA -- it shows where Hilton's profit, not just its revenue, actually comes from.

For Hilton: management & franchise fees carry far higher margins than owned-hotel operations, so this split should show an even more lopsided mix than segment revenue -- that margin gap is why the market prices Hilton as a fee business rather than a hotel owner. FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA is guided to $4.06B-$4.08B.

What to watch:

  • Management & franchise EBITDA margin (vs its revenue) widening further as the mix shifts
  • Ownership segment EBITDA swings -- a handful of owned hotels can move this line disproportionately

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
